patient_information: A 35-year-old Caucasian male with an unremarkable past medical history.
chief_complaint: Fatigue and a rash on his neck that started as a papule 2 days earlier.
history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a rash on his neck that began as a papule two days prior. The lesion was non-pruritic but was associated with significant, non-painful swelling and a pressure sensation in the neck. He reported no fever, but had at least one episode of diaphoresis with mild confusion and headache. He recalled a break in the skin at the site three days before the lesion appeared while shaving. He had been seen 24 hours earlier for similar symptoms, was given a cephalosporin, and discharged, but returned due to worsening malaise, increased neck swelling, and mild difficulty breathing.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a postal worker in the United States. He denied any foreign travel within the previous year, contact with animals, or insect bites. The presentation occurred during an investigation into a possible bioterrorism event. It was later confirmed that he was exposed during his occupation while handling contaminated mail.
vitals: Temperature was 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse was 118 bpm, blood pressure was 138/90 mmHg, and the respiratory rate was 20 breaths per minute.
physical_exam: Examination revealed a 2cm irregularly shaped, indurated, non-tender patch on the left anterior neck with mild erythema and several 2-3mm vesicles. The main lesion had a 6mm shallow ulceration. There was massive neck oedema, with neck circumference increased from a baseline of 57cm to 81cm, making lymph nodes difficult to assess. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial blood work, including full blood count and chemistries, was normal except for a mildly elevated haemoglobin at 18.7 g/dL. Blood cultures taken at the first clinic visit grew gram-positive rods. Gram stain and culture from the skin lesion were negative for B. anthracis. A full-thickness skin biopsy performed at a reference laboratory showed abundant bacilli in the dermis, and immunohistochemical (IHC) staining detected B. anthracis antigens. Convalescent serology revealed the presence of antibody to protective antigen.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnosis for an ulcerative skin lesion with massive soft tissue swelling included bacterial ecthyma (Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus), rickettsial diseases, necrotic arachnidism, rat-bite fevers, ulceroglandular tularemia, and bubonic plague. Given the context of a possible bioterrorism event in the United States at the time, cutaneous anthrax was considered the most important diagnosis.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was initially treated with a first-generation cephalosporin but his condition worsened. Upon hospital admission, he received intravenous levofloxacin and ampicillin-sulbactam and subsequently recovered.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis. Although the direct culture of the skin lesion was negative, the diagnosis was confirmed by several key findings. Blood cultures grew gram-positive rods. A skin biopsy showed abundant bacilli, and immunohistochemical staining was positive for B. anthracis antigens. Furthermore, serology on convalescent serum was positive for antibodies to the protective antigen. The exposure was determined to be occupational, from handling contaminated mail during a bioterrorism event.
